# Role

# Task

# Overall Article Context
**Article Topic:** What are the causes, variations, and historical shifts in the life expectancy gap between women and men worldwide?

**Overall Requirements:**
- How and why do women tend to live longer than men across countries?
- What factors contribute to the sex gap in life expectancy at different ages?
- How has the sex gap in life expectancy changed over time and what explains these shifts?

# Current Section Information

**Section Description:** This section introduces the persistent global phenomenon that women tend to live longer than men, quantifies the current gap in life expectancy, and frames the central questions the article will address: the origins, variability, and historical changes of the sex gap in life expectancy.

**Section Requirements (must address all):**
- Women have a higher average life expectancy than men globally, with a 5-year gap in 2021.
- The article will explore whether the gap is due to differences at old ages or higher risks for young men.

Women tend to live longer than men. In 2021, this difference amounted to a [5-year gap]() in global life expectancy: the average life expectancy was 73.8 years for women versus 68.4 years for men.
[Source txt1 end]

[Source txt2 begin]
[5]() Within racial groups, women tend to live longer than men: On average, women’s life expectancy exceeds that of men of the same race by about five years, with a somewhat larger difference between black women and black men.
[Source txt2 end]

[Source txt3 begin]
Women live longer than men almost everywhere. Nowadays, they not only have longer life expectancy, but they have lower mortality throughout the age spectrum, with some exceptions regarding maternal mortality, especially in the past (Loudon, [1988]( "Loudon, I. \(1988\). Maternal mortality: 1880–1950. Some regional and international comparisons. Social History of Medicine, 1, 183–228.")), and childhood mortality (for example, for ages 0 to 4 in 2021, in Algeria, Bangladesh, Egypt, India, and Iran female mortality was higher than male childhood mortality) (Chao et al., [2023]( "Chao, F., Masquelier, B., You, D., Hug, L., Liu, Y., Sharrow, D., Rue, H., Ombao, H., Alkema, L., & Cao, B. \(2023\). Sex differences in mortality among children, adolescents, and young people aged 0–24 years: A systematic assessment of national, regional, and global trends from 1990 to 2021. The Lancet Global Health, 11, e1519–e1530.")). Such mortality differences, as well as a skewed sex ratio at birth towards the male sex (Beltrán Tapia & Raftakis, [2022]( "Beltrán Tapia, H., & Raftakis, M. \(2022\). Sex ratios and gender discrimination in Modern Greece. Population Studies, 76, 329–346."); Bongaarts, [2013]( "Bongaarts, J. \(2013\). The implementation of preferences for male offspring. Population and Development Review, 39, 185–208."); Das Gupta & Mari Bhat, [1997]( "Das Gupta, M., & Mari Bhat, P. N. \(1997\). Fertility decline and increased manifestation of sex bias in India. Population Studies., 51, 307–315."); Guilmoto [2009]( "Guilmoto, C. Z. \(2009\). The sex ratio transition in Asia. Population and Development Review, 35, 519–549."); Guilmoto [2012]( "Guilmoto, C. Z. \(2012\). Skewed sex ratios at birth and future marriage squeeze in China and India, 2005–2100. Demography, 49, 77–100.")), highlight the potential presence of gender-based discrimination practices.
[Source txt3 end]

[Source txt4 begin]
## Introduction
On average and worldwide, women live longer than men (Austad, [2006]( "Austad, S. N. \(2006\). Why women live longer than men: Sex differences in longevity. Sex Medicine, 3\(2\), 79–92.
)80198-1
[Source txt4 end]

[Source txt5 begin]
_Today women live longer than men virtually in every country of the world. Although scientists still struggle to fully explain this disparity, the most prominent sources of this gender inequality are biological and behavioral. From an evolutionary point of view, female longevity was more advantageous for offspring survival. This resulted in a higher frequency of non-fatal diseases among women and in a later onset of fatal conditions. The observed high variation in the longevity gap across countries, however, points towards an important role of social and behavioral arguments. These include higher consumption of alcohol, tobacco, and fats among men as well as a generally riskier behavior. The gender gap in life expectancy often reaches 6-12 percent of the average human lifespan and has remained stubbornly stable in many countries. Lower life expectancy among men is an important social concern on its own and has significant consequences for the well-being of their surviving partners and the economy as a whole. It is an important, yet under-discussed type of gender inequality._
[Source txt5 end]

[Source txt6 begin]
It’s sustained at older ages when men have higher death rates than women from chronic health conditions, which are partly due to higher rates of smoking, alcohol, and drug use.
As there are many reasons for the sex gap in life expectancy, its size varies between countries and has shifted over time.
[Source txt6 end]

[Source txt7 begin]
In almost all human populations women live longer than men. In this study we found that the female survival advantage extends to seven documented populations experiencing high-mortality crises. Our results add another piece to the puzzle of gender differences in survival. They suggest that the female advantage stems from fundamental biological roots and is influenced by socially and environmentally determined risks, opportunities, and resources.
[Source txt7 end]

[Source txt8 begin]
Modern female human life expectancy is greater than that of males, despite females having higher morbidity rates (see [health survival paradox]( "Health survival paradox")). There are several potential reasons for this. Traditional arguments tend to favor sociology-environmental factors: historically, men have consumed more [tobacco]( "Tobacco"), [alcohol]( "Alcoholic drink"), and [drugs]( "Drug") than women in most societies, and are more likely to die from many associated diseases such as [lung cancer]( "Lung cancer"), [tuberculosis]( "Tuberculosis"), and [cirrhosis of the liver]( "Cirrhosis of the liver").[[84]]() Men are also more likely to die from injuries, whether unintentional (such as [occupational]( "Occupational safety and health"), [war]( "War"), or [car wrecks]( "Car wrecks")) or intentional ([suicide]( "Suicide")).[[84]]() Men are also more likely to die from the leading causes of death (some already stated) than women. Some of these in the United States include cancer of the respiratory system, motor vehicle accidents, suicide, cirrhosis of the liver, emphysema, prostate cancer, and coronary heart disease.[[14]]() These far outweigh the female mortality rate from breast cancer and cervical cancer. In the past, [mortality rates for females in child-bearing age groups]( "Maternal death") were higher than for males at the same age.
[Source txt8 end]

[Source txt9 begin]
Projected increases in longevity for both men and women would narrow the gap in life expectancy by sex to 3.4 years in 2060, nearly half of its historic high in the 1970s of 7.8 years (Figure 1). Despite projected improvements to life expectancy among men and women, men are still projected to have shorter life expectancy than women. Mortality differences between men and women are often attributed to differences in health and social behaviors such as smoking, drinking patterns, and exercise (Crimmins, Kim, and Solé- Auró, 2010; Rogers et al., 2010). In addition, the leading causes of death for men and women differ. While heart disease and cancer are the top two killers for both men and women, men are more likely to die from unintentional injuries, suicide, and chronic liver disease, whereas women have higher mortality burdens from stroke and kidney disease (Heron, 2019).
[Source txt9 end]

[Source txt10 begin]
#### Women tend to live longer than men, but this gap has changed over time
Across the world, [women tend to live longer than men]().
But the gender gap varies between countries and is not constant over time, as you can see in the chart.
For example, the gap spiked in some countries during the World Wars.
[Source txt10 end]

[Source txt11 begin]
Women consistently have higher life expectancies; however, their gains have happened more slowly than have men’s. In 1960, men could expect to live to age 66.6, on average, while women lived to age 73.1 (Figure 1). Between 1960 and 2015, male life expectancy increased to 77.0 years—a gain of about 10 years. Female life expectancy grew to 81.7 years— an increase of almost 9 years. By 2060, males are projected to live to be 83.9 years old—a gain of
[Source txt11 end]

[Source txt12 begin]
. Accessed May 2015")). The reasons for this gender difference are thought to have both biological and non-biological origins. Biological differences in genetic structure and hormones are suggested to favor female life expectancy (Luy and Wegner-Siegmundt [2015]( "Luy M, Wegner-Siegmundt C \(2015\) The impact of smoking on gender differences in life expectancy: more heterogeneous than often stated. Eur J Public Health 25:706–710"); Oksuzyan et al. [2008]( "Oksuzyan A, Juel K, Vaupel JW, Christensen K \(2008\) Men: good health and high mortality. Sex differences in health and aging. Aging Clin Exp Res 20:91–102")). However, several studies have attributed the bulk (> 75%) of the gender gap in life expectancy to non-biological factors (e.g., behavior, life style, social roles) (Luy and Wegner-Siegmundt [2015]( "Luy M, Wegner-Siegmundt C \(2015\) The impact of smoking on gender differences in life expectancy: more heterogeneous than often stated. Eur J Public Health 25:706–710"); Oksuzyan et al. [2008]( "Oksuzyan A, Juel K, Vaupel JW, Christensen K \(2008\) Men: good health and high mortality. Sex differences in health and aging. Aging Clin Exp Res 20:91–102")), with higher mortality risk among men due to smoking, hazardous alcohol consumption, substance abuse and occupational risks (Loef and Walach [2012]( "Loef M, Walach H \(2012\) The combined effects of healthy lifestyle behaviors on all cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Prev Med 55:163–170"); Oksuzyan et al. [2008]( "Oksuzyan A, Juel K, Vaupel JW, Christensen K \(2008\) Men: good health and high mortality. Sex differences in health and aging. Aging Clin Exp Res 20:91–102")). A recent paper addressing the gender gap in life expectancy in Sweden also points to social change as a main driver of the historically observed changes in the gender gap (Hemström [2016]( "Hemström Ö \(2016\) Changes in the gender gap in life expectancy in Sweden: A cohort analysis with the most recent trends. In: Dinges M, Weigl A \(eds\) Gender-specific Life Expectancy in Europe 1850–2010. Franz Steiner Verlag")). As for the currently ongoing decrease of the gender gap in life expectancy, there is some evidence suggesting that it could mostly be attributed to changing gender patterns of smoking (Pampel [2002]( "Pampel FC \(2002\) Cigarette use and the narrowing sex differential in mortality. Popul Dev Rev 28:77–104"), [2005]( "Pampel FC \(2005\) Forecasting sex differences in mortality in high income nations: the contribution of smoking. Demogr Res 13:455")); specifically, an increase in smoking among women and subsequent delayed health consequences (Lopez et al. [1994]( "Lopez AD, Collishaw NE, Piha T \(1994\) A descriptive model of the cigarette epidemic in developed countries. Tob Control 3:242"); Pampel [2006]( "Pampel FC \(2006\) Global patterns and determinants of sex differences in smoking. Int J Comp Sociol 47:466–487")). The gender gap in Sweden is one of Europe’s lowest (Van Oyen et al. [2013]( "Van Oyen H, Nusselder W, Jagger C, Kolip P, Cambois E, Robine JM \(2013\) Gender differences in healthy life years within the EU: an exploration of the “health-survival” paradox. Int J Public Health 58:143–155.
[Source txt12 end]

[Source txt13 begin]
The scientific community has been lively debating for a long time about the factors that might be determining this survival advantage, which has been traditionally explained both from biological and socio/behavioral factors (Austad & Fischer, [2016]( "Austad, S. N., & Fischer, K. E. \(2016\). Sex differences in lifespan. Cell Metabolism, 23, 1022–1033."); Luy & Wegner-Siegmundt, [2015]( "Luy, M., & Wegner-Siegmundt, C. \(2015\). The impact of smoking on gender differences in life expectancy: More heterogeneous than often stated. The European Journal of Public Health, 25, 706–710."); Rogers et al., [2010]( "Rogers, R. G., Everett, B. G., Onge, J. M. S., & Krueger, P. M. \(2010\). Social, behavioral, and biological factors, and sex differences in mortality. Demography, 47, 555–578.")). Biological factors pertain to the different biological endowments which would characterize females compared with males. Behavioral explanations, instead, point towards smoking or alcohol and drug abuse and, more reckless behavior typical of males. It is not always easy to clearly disentangle these factors. For example, reckless behaviors could be partly attributed to gender roles and masculinity of which the socialization of young adult males is permeated (Courtenay, [2000]( "Courtenay, W. H. \(2000\). Constructions of masculinity and their influence on men’s well-being: A theory of gender and health. Social Science & Medicine, 50, 1385–1401.")), and partly to testosterone surges, even though it is not clear if high testosterone is the consequence, rather than the cause, of aggressive and risky behaviors and situations (Archer, [2006]( "Archer, J. \(2006\). Testosterone and human aggression: An evaluation of the challenge hypothesis. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 30, 319–345."); Casto & Edwards, [2016]( "Casto, K. V., & Edwards, D. A. \(2016\). Testosterone, cortisol, and human competition. Hormones and Behavior, 82, 21–37."); Mehta & Josephs, [2006]( "Mehta, P. H., & Josephs, R. A. \(2006\). Testosterone change after losing predicts the decision to compete again. Hormones and Behavior, 50, 684–692.")). To further increase the confusion, there is also the evidence that a pronounced female survival advantage as we know it today seems to have emerged during the late nineteenth and early twentieth century (Beltrán-Sánchez et al., [2015]( "Beltrán-Sánchez, H., Finch, C. E., & Crimmins, E. M. \(2015\). Twentieth century surge of excess adult male mortality. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112, 8993–8998.")). On the other hand, evidence exist on what can be defined as some innate biological better ability to survive of female infants over male infants way back in the past and when mortality conditions were much worse than today’s. The analysis of Salinari et al. ([2022]( "Salinari, G., de Santis, G., Zarulli, V., Giuliani, C., Franceschi, C., & Breschi, M. \(2022\). Fertility decline and the emergence of excess female survival in post-reproductive ages in Italy. Genus, 78, 19.")) contributes to the debate by testing, in the Italian context, an innovative hypothesis that, as of today, has been scrutinized only in a handful of studies (Bolund et al., [2016]( "Bolund, E., Lummaa, V., Smith, K. R., Hanson, H. A., & Maklakov, A. A. \(2016\). Reduced costs of reproduction in females mediate a shift from a male-biased to a female-biased lifespan in humans. Scientific Reports, 6, 24672."); Gagnon et al., [2009]( "Gagnon, A., Smith, K. R., Tremblay, M., Vézina, H., Paré, P. P., & Desjardins, B. \(2009\). Is there a trade-off between fertility and longevity? A comparative study of women from three large historical databases accounting for mortality selection. American Journal of Human Biology: THe Official Journal of the Human Biology Association, 21, 533–540."); Helle & Lummaa, [2013]( "Helle, S., & Lummaa, V. \(2013\). A trade-off between having many sons and shorter maternal post-reproductive survival in pre-industrial Finland. Biology Letters, 9, 20130034."); Hurt et al., [2006]( "Hurt, L. S., Ronsmans, C., & Thomas, S. L. \(2006\). The effect of number of births on women’s mortality: Systematic review of the evidence for women who have completed their childbearing. Population Studies, 60, 55–71."); Jasienska, [2009]( "Jasienska, G. \(2009\). Reproduction and lifespan: Trade-offs, overall energy budgets, intergenerational costs, and costs neglected by research. American Journal of Human Biology: THe Official Journal of the Human Biology Association, 21, 524–532."); Le Bourg, [2007]( "Le Bourg, E. \(2007\). Does reproduction decrease longevity in human beings? Ageing Research Reviews., 6, 141–149.")): the idea that women’s mortality advantage might have emerged thanks to historical process of decreasing fertility during the demographic transition, in a context of trade-off between survival and reproduction. To test this hypothesis, the authors of the study analyzed various survival indicators at post-reproductive ages of pre- and post-transitional cohorts of women, based on their completed fertility histories and found that large progenies (and, to a lesser extent, childlessness) lead to lower survival chances, and that this relationship was strong enough to affect the female-to-male ratio in old age as fertility declined.
[Source txt13 end]

[Source txt14 begin]
Women are the life-expectancy champions: They can expect to live longer than men almost anywhere in the world today ([1]()–[3]()). This pervasive inequality has intrigued researchers for decades ([4]()). The cumulative corpus of research supports the conclusion that the gap has biological underpinnings modulated by social and environmental conditions. Deeper understanding could benefit from biodemographic research ([5]()). Here we present some results of such research.
[Source txt14 end]

[Source txt15 begin]
On the other hand, women, on average, are more cautious than men, and are known to adopt healthier habits and lifestyles: they tend to follow a healthier diet, consume less alcohol, smoke less, and adhere more closely to health recommendations (Rogers et al., [2010]( "Rogers, R. G., Everett, B. G., Onge, J. M. S., & Krueger, P. M. \(2010\). Social, behavioral, and biological factors, and sex differences in mortality. Demography, 47, 555–578.")). However, a female survival advantage has been observed also in religious populations where both sexes share similar and healthier lifestyles compared to the general population (Lindahl-Jacobsen et al., [2013]( "Lindahl-Jacobsen, R., Hanson, H. A., Oksuzyan, A., Mineau, G. P., Christensen, K., & Smith, K. R. \(2013\). The male–female health-survival paradox and sex differences in cohort life expectancy in Utah, Denmark, and Sweden 1850–1910. Annals of Epidemiology, 23, 161–166."); Luy, [2003]( "Luy, M. \(2003\). Causes of male excess mortality: Insights from cloistered populations. Population and Development Review, 29, 647–676.")); furthermore, the ages when the recklessness of men peaks, that is, the young adult ages of the famous (among demographers) accident hump (Goldstein, [2011]( "Goldstein, J. R. \(2011\). A secular trend toward earlier male sexual maturity: Evidence from shifting ages of male young adult mortality. PLoS ONE, 6, e14826."); Remund et al., [2018]( "Remund, A., Camarda, C. G., & Riffe, T. \(2018\). A cause-of-death decomposition of young adult excess mortality. Demography, 55, 957–978.")), have been showed to contribute very little to the overall gender gap in life expectancy, both in modern and historical populations (Zarulli et al., [2021]( "Zarulli, V., Kashnitsky, I., & Vaupel, J. W. \(2021\). Death rates at specific life stages mold the sex gap in life expectancy. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 118, e2010588118.")).
[Source txt15 end]

[Source txt16 begin]
### Why do women live longer than men?
Women tend to live longer than men in all countries — but the sex gap in life expectancy is not a constant.
]()
[Source txt16 end]

[Source txt17 begin]
In every country in the world, [women tend to live longer than men](). Whilst this is true today, it hasn't always been the case.
In our article "[Why do women live longer than men?]()", we take a look at the data and explanations for why this is the case.
[
![Thumbnail for article on sex gap in life expectancy]()
[Source txt17 end]

[Source txt18 begin]
Life expectancy (LE) has increased worldwide and steadily in developed countries, such as the UK [[1]()]. This improvement draws special attention to their high-quality health systems regarding disease control, treatment, and prevention, among other population inherited characteristics [[2]()]. An average citizen in the UK should live until the age of 81.3 years under the current age-specific death rates [[3]()]. However, women outlive men. Even though this gender gap in LE (GGLE) has been declining over the last 20 years, there is still 3.7 years of difference in the GGLE observed in 2019 compared to 4.8 years in the early 2000s [[4](), [5]()]. Different explanations have been suggested for this GGLE including biological features (e.g. quantity of chromosomes, iron levels, and hormone disorders and triggers), behavioural (e.g. habits, lifestyle, and physical activity), health risk factors (e.g. alcohol consumption, smoking, obesity), and sociodemographic characteristics (e.g. risky jobs and sociocultural roles) [[6](), [7]()]. While men have been historically linked to more hazardous occupations (e.g. manual and elementary labours), the situation is changing with turndown of the mining and manufacturing industries together with an accelerated eradication of physical labours, as well as a reduced smoking prevalence among men [[8](), [9]()]. Simultaneously, women have increased their health risky behaviour (such as alcohol consumption, smoking, and obesity), reaching similar levels to that of men [[8](), [10]()]. All these patterns have likely contributed to the reduction in GGLE over the recent years in many countries around the world [[11](), [12]()].
[Source txt18 end]

[Source txt19 begin]
Women lived longer than men in almost all populations, and higher proportions of women than men survived from birth to each age ([Fig. 1]()). The female survival curves were higher than the male ones at all ages, with the exception of the Trinidad slaves. Here survival was higher for men than for women until age 50 y in the lower-bound scenario or until age 25 y in the upper-bound scenario, as a consequence of the higher female mortality in childhood and at young adult ages.
[Source txt19 end]

[Source txt20 begin]
Gender inequalities across the world make women and girls more vulnerable to poor health, often putting them at higher risks of death, including from a maternal cause. At the global level, however, women live on average longer than men (table II.2). Higher male mortality has been associated with behavioural factors and genetic differences (Austad, 2006). In 2021, life expectancy at birth for women exceeded that for men by 5.4 years globally, with female and male life expectancies standing at 73.8 and 68.4, respectively. This female survival advantage is observed in virtually all regions and countries of the world. The female advantage in life expectancy at birth ranged from 7 years in Latin America and the Caribbean to 2.9 years in Australia and New Zealand. The COVID-19 pandemic contributed to widening the gap in life expectancy at birth between sexes. In 2019, this gap reached 5.2 years. In the last three decades, the sex gap in life expectancy at birth shrank in some regions (Australia and New Zealand, Europe and Northern America), but increased in others (Central and Southern Asia, and Eastern and South-Eastern Asia) (United Nations, 2020a). In subSaharan Africa, the rise in the sex differential of life expectancy at birth was interrupted in the late 1990s due to the disproportionate impact of the HIV/AIDS epidemic on female mortality in that region, which had its maximum effect on mortality rates in the mid-2000s. The COVID-19 pandemic contributed to a slight increase in the gap in life expectancy at birth between the sexes.
[Source txt20 end]

# The Global Phenomenon of Women Living Longer Than Men

Across the globe, one of the most consistent demographic patterns is that women tend to live longer than men. In 2021, this difference amounted to a significant 5-year gap in global life expectancy: the average life expectancy was 73.8 years for women versus 68.4 years for men [citation:txt1]. This phenomenon is not limited to a few countries or regions but is observed almost universally [citation:txt3]. Even within racial groups, women tend to outlive men by about five years, with some of the largest differences seen between Black women and Black men [citation:txt2].

The persistence of this gender gap in life expectancy raises a number of compelling questions. Why do women consistently live longer than men? What factors contribute to this disparity, and how do they vary across age groups and geographic regions? Has the gap always been this wide, or has it changed over time? These are the central questions this article will address, exploring the origins, variability, and historical shifts in the sex gap in life expectancy.

The sex gap in life expectancy is not solely a result of differences at older ages, where men typically experience higher mortality rates due to chronic health conditions such as heart disease and cancer [citation:txt6]. While these factors are significant, the gap is also influenced by higher risks for young men, particularly in terms of behavioral and environmental factors such as smoking, alcohol use, and risky behaviors [citation:txt5]. Moreover, some of the mortality differences can be traced back to childhood, with female mortality being higher than male in certain regions for ages 0 to 4 [citation:txt3]. These early-life disparities, along with skewed sex ratios at birth in some parts of the world, further complicate the picture [citation:txt3].

Understanding the sex gap in life expectancy requires a multifaceted approach, as both biological and social factors play roles in shaping this inequality. Some researchers argue that evolutionary advantages in female longevity have contributed to the survival of women over men, particularly in post-reproductive years [citation:txt13]. Others emphasize the impact of social and behavioral factors, such as men's higher rates of smoking, drinking, and exposure to occupational risks [citation:txt8]. As the following sections will explore in greater depth, the interplay of these factors varies across countries and historical periods, making the sex gap in life expectancy a complex and evolving phenomenon.

The scientific community has been lively debating for a long time about the factors that might be determining this survival advantage, which has been traditionally explained both from biological and socio/behavioral factors (Austad & Fischer, [2016]( "Austad, S. N., & Fischer, K. E. \(2016\). Sex differences in lifespan. Cell Metabolism, 23, 1022–1033."); Luy & Wegner-Siegmundt, [2015]( "Luy, M., & Wegner-Siegmundt, C. \(2015\). The impact of smoking on gender differences in life expectancy: More heterogeneous than often stated. The European Journal of Public Health, 25, 706–710."); Rogers et al., [2010]( "Rogers, R. G., Everett, B. G., Onge, J. M. S., & Krueger, P. M. \(2010\). Social, behavioral, and biological factors, and sex differences in mortality. Demography, 47, 555–578.")). Biological factors pertain to the different biological endowments which would characterize females compared with males. Behavioral explanations, instead, point towards smoking or alcohol and drug abuse and, more reckless behavior typical of males. It is not always easy to clearly disentangle these factors. For example, reckless behaviors could be partly attributed to gender roles and masculinity of which the socialization of young adult males is permeated (Courtenay, [2000]( "Courtenay, W. H. \(2000\). Constructions of masculinity and their influence on men’s well-being: A theory of gender and health. Social Science & Medicine, 50, 1385–1401.")), and partly to testosterone surges, even though it is not clear if high testosterone is the consequence, rather than the cause, of aggressive and risky behaviors and situations (Archer, [2006]( "Archer, J. \(2006\). Testosterone and human aggression: An evaluation of the challenge hypothesis. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 30, 319–345."); Casto & Edwards, [2016]( "Casto, K. V., & Edwards, D. A. \(2016\). Testosterone, cortisol, and human competition. Hormones and Behavior, 82, 21–37."); Mehta & Josephs, [2006]( "Mehta, P. H., & Josephs, R. A. \(2006\). Testosterone change after losing predicts the decision to compete again. Hormones and Behavior, 50, 684–692.")). To further increase the confusion, there is also the evidence that a pronounced female survival advantage as we know it today seems to have emerged during the late nineteenth and early twentieth century (Beltrán-Sánchez et al., [2015]( "Beltrán-Sánchez, H., Finch, C. E., & Crimmins, E. M. \(2015\). Twentieth century surge of excess adult male mortality. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112, 8993–8998.")). On the other hand, evidence exist on what can be defined as some innate biological better ability to survive of female infants over male infants way back in the past and when mortality conditions were much worse than today’s. The analysis of Salinari et al. ([2022]( "Salinari, G., de Santis, G., Zarulli, V., Giuliani, C., Franceschi, C., & Breschi, M. \(2022\). Fertility decline and the emergence of excess female survival in post-reproductive ages in Italy. Genus, 78, 19.")) contributes to the debate by testing, in the Italian context, an innovative hypothesis that, as of today, has been scrutinized only in a handful of studies (Bolund et al., [2016]( "Bolund, E., Lummaa, V., Smith, K. R., Hanson, H. A., & Maklakov, A. A. \(2016\). Reduced costs of reproduction in females mediate a shift from a male-biased to a female-biased lifespan in humans. Scientific Reports, 6, 24672."); Gagnon et al., [2009]( "Gagnon, A., Smith, K. R., Tremblay, M., Vézina, H., Paré, P. P., & Desjardins, B. \(2009\). Is there a trade-off between fertility and longevity? A comparative study of women from three large historical databases accounting for mortality selection. American Journal of Human Biology: THe Official Journal of the Human Biology Association, 21, 533–540."); Helle & Lummaa, [2013]( "Helle, S., & Lummaa, V. \(2013\). A trade-off between having many sons and shorter maternal post-reproductive survival in pre-industrial Finland. Biology Letters, 9, 20130034."); Hurt et al., [2006]( "Hurt, L. S., Ronsmans, C., & Thomas, S. L. \(2006\). The effect of number of births on women’s mortality: Systematic review of the evidence for women who have completed their childbearing. Population Studies, 60, 55–71."); Jasienska, [2009]( "Jasienska, G. \(2009\). Reproduction and lifespan: Trade-offs, overall energy budgets, intergenerational costs, and costs neglected by research. American Journal of Human Biology: THe Official Journal of the Human Biology Association, 21, 524–532."); Le Bourg, [2007]( "Le Bourg, E. \(2007\). Does reproduction decrease longevity in human beings? Ageing Research Reviews., 6, 141–149.")): the idea that women’s mortality advantage might have emerged thanks to historical process of decreasing fertility during the demographic transition, in a context of trade-off between survival and reproduction. To test this hypothesis, the authors of the study analyzed various survival indicators at post-reproductive ages of pre- and post-transitional cohorts of women, based on their completed fertility histories and found that large progenies (and, to a lesser extent, childlessness) lead to lower survival chances, and that this relationship was strong enough to affect the female-to-male ratio in old age as fertility declined.

[5]() Within racial groups, women tend to live longer than men: On average, women’s life expectancy exceeds that of men of the same race by about five years, with a somewhat larger difference between black women and black men.

Women live longer than men almost everywhere. Nowadays, they not only have longer life expectancy, but they have lower mortality throughout the age spectrum, with some exceptions regarding maternal mortality, especially in the past (Loudon, [1988]( "Loudon, I. \(1988\). Maternal mortality: 1880–1950. Some regional and international comparisons. Social History of Medicine, 1, 183–228.")), and childhood mortality (for example, for ages 0 to 4 in 2021, in Algeria, Bangladesh, Egypt, India, and Iran female mortality was higher than male childhood mortality) (Chao et al., [2023]( "Chao, F., Masquelier, B., You, D., Hug, L., Liu, Y., Sharrow, D., Rue, H., Ombao, H., Alkema, L., & Cao, B. \(2023\). Sex differences in mortality among children, adolescents, and young people aged 0–24 years: A systematic assessment of national, regional, and global trends from 1990 to 2021. The Lancet Global Health, 11, e1519–e1530.")). Such mortality differences, as well as a skewed sex ratio at birth towards the male sex (Beltrán Tapia & Raftakis, [2022]( "Beltrán Tapia, H., & Raftakis, M. \(2022\). Sex ratios and gender discrimination in Modern Greece. Population Studies, 76, 329–346."); Bongaarts, [2013]( "Bongaarts, J. \(2013\). The implementation of preferences for male offspring. Population and Development Review, 39, 185–208."); Das Gupta & Mari Bhat, [1997]( "Das Gupta, M., & Mari Bhat, P. N. \(1997\). Fertility decline and increased manifestation of sex bias in India. Population Studies., 51, 307–315."); Guilmoto [2009]( "Guilmoto, C. Z. \(2009\). The sex ratio transition in Asia. Population and Development Review, 35, 519–549."); Guilmoto [2012]( "Guilmoto, C. Z. \(2012\). Skewed sex ratios at birth and future marriage squeeze in China and India, 2005–2100. Demography, 49, 77–100.")), highlight the potential presence of gender-based discrimination practices.

_Today women live longer than men virtually in every country of the world. Although scientists still struggle to fully explain this disparity, the most prominent sources of this gender inequality are biological and behavioral. From an evolutionary point of view, female longevity was more advantageous for offspring survival. This resulted in a higher frequency of non-fatal diseases among women and in a later onset of fatal conditions. The observed high variation in the longevity gap across countries, however, points towards an important role of social and behavioral arguments. These include higher consumption of alcohol, tobacco, and fats among men as well as a generally riskier behavior. The gender gap in life expectancy often reaches 6-12 percent of the average human lifespan and has remained stubbornly stable in many countries. Lower life expectancy among men is an important social concern on its own and has significant consequences for the well-being of their surviving partners and the economy as a whole. It is an important, yet under-discussed type of gender inequality._

It’s sustained at older ages when men have higher death rates than women from chronic health conditions, which are partly due to higher rates of smoking, alcohol, and drug use.
As there are many reasons for the sex gap in life expectancy, its size varies between countries and has shifted over time.

Modern female human life expectancy is greater than that of males, despite females having higher morbidity rates (see [health survival paradox]( "Health survival paradox")). There are several potential reasons for this. Traditional arguments tend to favor sociology-environmental factors: historically, men have consumed more [tobacco]( "Tobacco"), [alcohol]( "Alcoholic drink"), and [drugs]( "Drug") than women in most societies, and are more likely to die from many associated diseases such as [lung cancer]( "Lung cancer"), [tuberculosis]( "Tuberculosis"), and [cirrhosis of the liver]( "Cirrhosis of the liver").[[84]]() Men are also more likely to die from injuries, whether unintentional (such as [occupational]( "Occupational safety and health"), [war]( "War"), or [car wrecks]( "Car wrecks")) or intentional ([suicide]( "Suicide")).[[84]]() Men are also more likely to die from the leading causes of death (some already stated) than women. Some of these in the United States include cancer of the respiratory system, motor vehicle accidents, suicide, cirrhosis of the liver, emphysema, prostate cancer, and coronary heart disease.[[14]]() These far outweigh the female mortality rate from breast cancer and cervical cancer. In the past, [mortality rates for females in child-bearing age groups]( "Maternal death") were higher than for males at the same age.

# Variability of the Sex Gap in Life Expectancy Across Countries and Time

While the global pattern of women outliving men is consistent, the size of the life expectancy gap varies significantly across countries and has evolved over time. In 2021, for example, the gender gap in life expectancy at birth averaged 5.4 years across OECD countries, with notable differences between regions. Central and Eastern European countries like Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland experienced the largest gaps, with women living eight or more years longer than men, while countries such as Iceland and Norway had much narrower gaps, at three years or less [citation:txt1]. These disparities reflect a complex interplay of historical, social, and health-related factors.

Historical events have played a crucial role in shaping the sex gap in life expectancy. Major conflicts such as wars have led to temporary but significant increases in male mortality, thereby widening the gap. For instance, during the 20th century, the life expectancy gap in many countries widened due to the high toll of wars on male populations. In Russia, the gap in life expectancy between women and men reached as high as 12 to 14 years in the 1990s, a period marked by economic and social upheaval following the dissolution of the Soviet Union [citation:txt6]. Similarly, the United States saw a peak in the sex gap at the end of the 1970s, while Sweden reached its peak in 1980 [citation:txt20]. These spikes underscore how external shocks can have long-lasting effects on demographic trends.

The 20th century also witnessed a general widening of the sex gap in life expectancy, particularly in industrialized nations. From the 1920s to the 1970s, the gap increased steadily in most developed countries due to rising male mortality from causes such as tobacco and alcohol use, occupational hazards, and higher rates of violent deaths [citation:txt17]. However, this trend began to reverse in the 1980s, especially in Western Europe, where the gap started to narrow. The decline in the sex gap has been attributed to improvements in public health, reductions in risky male behaviors, and greater access to healthcare for men. For example, in Japan, the gap peaked in the early 2000s but has since decreased, reflecting broader societal changes in health and lifestyle [citation:txt8].

More recently, the gap has continued to shrink in many countries, although the pace and extent of this narrowing differ. From 2002 to 2016, the sex gap in life expectancy in Western European countries decreased by an average of 18.0%, the most significant reduction observed among the regions studied [citation:txt4]. The United Kingdom, for instance, saw the gap drop from 4.5 years to 3.5 years over this period. In contrast, countries in Eastern Europe, such as Russia, experienced smaller reductions, with the gap decreasing from 11.2 years in 2014 to 8.7 years on average by 2021 [citation:txt5]. The United States, while showing some decline, still maintains a larger gap than most comparable countries, with a 5.3-year difference between women and men as of 2023 [citation:txt11].

These variations can also be visualized in global data. The map of the 2023 sex gap in life expectancy highlights countries with the largest and smallest disparities [citation:img7]. Russia, Belarus, and Ukraine stand out for their large gaps, with female life expectancy exceeding male life expectancy by more than 10 years. In contrast, countries in Asia and parts of Africa exhibit much smaller gaps, with some, like Nepal and Pakistan, showing differences of less than half a year [citation:txt12]. Such data illustrate how the sex gap is not a fixed phenomenon but one that is shaped by local conditions, including healthcare infrastructure, cultural norms, and economic development.

The historical trajectory of the sex gap in life expectancy thus reveals a dynamic interplay between biological, behavioral, and environmental factors. While the gap has generally narrowed in recent decades, it remains a significant public health and social issue, particularly in regions where male mortality is disproportionately high. Understanding these patterns is essential for developing targeted interventions aimed at reducing gender disparities in health outcomes and promoting longevity for all.

# Understanding Period Life Expectancy and Its Influences

Period life expectancy is a statistical measure that summarizes the average number of years a person is expected to live based on the current age-specific death rates in a given year. It does not predict the actual lifespan of individuals but rather provides a snapshot of mortality conditions at a specific point in time. This metric is calculated by applying current death rates across all age groups to a hypothetical cohort of individuals born in that year, estimating how long they would live under those same conditions throughout their lives [citation:txt2].

Period life expectancy is highly sensitive to changes in health, behavior, and major historical events. For example, during wars or pandemics, life expectancy can drop significantly due to the increased mortality rates. The global HIV/AIDS epidemic in the late 20th century and the recent impact of the COVID-19 pandemic have both had measurable effects on life expectancy, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and other regions with vulnerable health systems [citation:txt7]. Similarly, improvements in healthcare, sanitation, and public health policies have historically led to increases in life expectancy, as seen in the post-World War II period in many developed countries [citation:txt20].

It is important to note that period life expectancy reflects average differences between populations and does not imply that all individuals within a group will experience the same outcomes. While women, on average, live longer than men globally, there are still many men who outlive women in their respective populations. This variation is influenced by a complex interplay of biological, behavioral, and sociocultural factors that affect individual health outcomes [citation:txt11]. For instance, some men may benefit from healthier lifestyles or better access to healthcare, while others may face unique risks that shorten their life expectancy [citation:txt13].

The data on life expectancy is also shaped by broader societal trends such as economic development, access to education, and gender roles. In wealthier nations, where healthcare systems are robust and preventive care is widely available, the gap between male and female life expectancy tends to be more pronounced. In contrast, in lower-income countries, especially those with high maternal and childhood mortality rates, the gap may be smaller or even reversed in some cases [citation:txt6]. As countries develop and adopt modern medical practices, the global trend has been toward a more consistent female advantage in life expectancy [citation:txt1].

As shown, both male and female life expectancies have increased over time, but the gap between the two has remained relatively stable. The data underscores the importance of understanding the factors that contribute to these differences, as well as the role of external events in shaping mortality patterns across populations [citation:txt3].

# The Age-Specific Sources of the Sex Gap in Life Expectancy

The sex gap in life expectancy is not a uniform phenomenon; it emerges and persists at different stages of the human lifespan. Males consistently exhibit higher death rates than females across infancy, youth, and older age, each contributing uniquely to the overall disparity in life expectancy. Understanding these age-specific patterns is essential for identifying the biological, behavioral, and social mechanisms that underpin the sex gap in mortality.

## Infant Mortality: Biological Vulnerabilities

Infant boys are biologically more vulnerable than girls, resulting in higher mortality rates during the first year of life. This disparity is evident globally and is rooted in a combination of genetic predispositions, higher susceptibility to infections, and complications related to prematurity. Before 1970, the primary causes of male infant mortality were infections and chronic degenerative diseases, but since then, improvements in medical care have disproportionately benefited male infants, narrowing the gap in some regions while highlighting persistent disparities in others [citation:txt12]. For example, in 2023, the infant mortality rates for boys exceeded those for girls in many African and Asian countries, with the Central African Republic and Niger showing some of the highest rates [![](citation:img1)].

## Youth Mortality: External Causes and Risk Behaviors

The sex gap in life expectancy widens significantly during youth, particularly between the ages of 15 and 49. During this stage, young men face a disproportionately higher risk of death from external causes such as accidents, violence, and suicide. In 2019, men and boys accounted for 80% of deaths due to homicide, 75% for road traffic injuries, and 69% for suicide [citation:txt2]. These trends are consistent across multiple regions, with the U.S., Russia, and Japan showing particularly stark differences in mortality rates between young men and women [citation:txt19]. Road traffic injuries remain the leading cause of death among boys and young men aged 15–29 years, while homicide ranks as the second leading cause in this age group [citation:txt2]. Additionally, global suicide mortality rates were 75% higher in men than in women in 2016, with transport-related deaths also showing a significant gender gap [![](citation:img10)].

## Older Age Mortality: Chronic Diseases and Risk Behaviors

In older age, the sex gap in life expectancy is sustained due to higher death rates in men from chronic diseases such as cardiovascular disease, cancer, and respiratory illnesses. These disparities are partly explained by long-standing differences in health behaviors, including higher rates of smoking, alcohol consumption, and sedentary lifestyles among men. For example, studies have shown that men are more likely to engage in risky behaviors such as heavy drinking and cigarette smoking, which contribute to elevated risks of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), liver cirrhosis, and coronary heart disease [citation:txt5]. In addition, men tend to delay seeking medical care and are less likely to adhere to preventive health measures, further exacerbating their mortality risk [citation:txt11]. 

The impact of these behaviors is reflected in mortality trends. For instance, in the U.S., age-standardized mortality rates for cardiovascular disease remain significantly higher among older men than women, with similar patterns observed in other high-income countries [![](citation:img5)]. Moreover, the decline in smoking rates among men over the past few decades has not kept pace with the reduction in rates among women, contributing to a persistent gap in life expectancy [citation:txt5].

## Conclusion of the Section

The sex gap in life expectancy is the cumulative result of higher male mortality rates at all stages of life. From the biological vulnerabilities of infant boys to the behavioral risks of young and older men, the factors contributing to this gap are complex and multifaceted. The following section will explore how these patterns vary across countries and how historical and social factors have shaped the sex gap in life expectancy over time.

# Historical Shifts in the Contributions of Different Age Groups to the Sex Gap in Life Expectancy

The sex gap in life expectancy has not remained static over time, nor has it been uniformly driven by the same age groups in different historical periods. Historically, infant mortality played a significant role in determining the life expectancy gap between men and women. In the early 20th century, for example, in countries such as France and Denmark, excess male infant deaths accounted for more than half of the overall sex gap in life expectancy [citation:txt19]. This was partly due to the biological vulnerability of male infants and also to underreporting of female infant deaths in some regions [citation:txt19]. However, as public health interventions improved and infant and child mortality rates declined, the contribution of early life stages to the sex gap diminished significantly [citation:txt17].

Instead, the sex gap has increasingly been influenced by mortality differences in middle and older age groups. For instance, in the United Kingdom, the sex gap at birth peaked in the 1940s, but the gap at older ages, such as 65 and 80, also grew significantly during this time. By the 21st century, while the overall sex gap had somewhat narrowed, the largest contributions to the gap came from older adults, with the 80+ age group accounting for a small but notable portion [citation:img1]. This trend is not unique to the UK. In many Western European countries, the United States, and Japan, the largest contributors to the sex gap in life expectancy have shifted to older age groups, particularly those over 70 years of age [citation:txt6].

This shift can be attributed to several factors. One major contributor has been the rise and subsequent decline in smoking rates among men. In the 20th century, the widespread adoption of smoking among men, particularly in industrialized countries, significantly widened the sex gap in life expectancy [citation:txt3]. Smoking-related diseases such as cardiovascular disease and lung cancer disproportionately affected male populations, especially in middle and older age [citation:txt7]. However, as anti-smoking campaigns and public health interventions took effect, mortality rates from smoking-related diseases have declined, particularly among older men, helping to narrow the sex gap [citation:txt3]. In the United States, for example, lung cancer death rates for men peaked in the 1990s and have since declined, while rates for women have also decreased but at a slower pace [citation:img7].

The impact of major historical events, particularly wars, cannot be overlooked. The World Wars, for instance, caused a dramatic spike in the sex gap due to the disproportionately high mortality of young and middle-aged men in combat. In the aftermath of these conflicts, the sex gap in life expectancy temporarily widened as a result of the large number of male deaths [citation:txt1]. This was particularly evident in countries such as Russia and Poland, where the gap in life expectancy between women and men remained large for decades due to high male mortality in youth and middle age [citation:txt6]. In these countries, the 60–79 age group continues to account for the most significant contribution to the sex gap in life expectancy [citation:img6].

Furthermore, the patterns of mortality contributions to the sex gap vary across countries. In Eastern European nations, for example, the largest contributions to the sex gap are still observed at relatively younger ages compared to Western European countries and the United States [citation:txt6]. In Russia, for instance, external causes of death—such as accidents, violence, and alcohol-related deaths—among men aged 25–30 and 40–45 years continue to play a major role in the large sex gap [citation:txt6]. These country-specific variations highlight the influence of social, economic, and cultural factors on mortality patterns and the life expectancy gap [citation:txt11].

In summary, the historical trajectory of the sex gap in life expectancy has been shaped by a complex interplay of biological, social, and medical factors. While infant and early childhood mortality once dominated the gap, the contributions of middle and older age groups have become more significant over time. The role of smoking, war-related mortality, and country-specific patterns of male mortality have all played critical roles in shaping these shifts. As public health interventions continue to evolve, understanding these historical trends remains essential for addressing the ongoing disparities in life expectancy between men and women.

# Summary and Conclusion

The sex gap in life expectancy is a persistent and multifaceted phenomenon that is evident from birth and continues throughout the lifespan. This gap is not uniform across countries or over time, and it is shaped by a complex interplay of biological, behavioral, and social factors. From the moment of birth, boys face higher mortality risks than girls, partly due to biological vulnerabilities such as genetic disorders and higher susceptibility to infections [citation:txt20]. These early differences set the stage for a lifelong disparity in life expectancy, which is further influenced by external and behavioral factors during youth and adulthood.

Historically, the primary contributor to the sex gap was infant mortality, with significant differences in survival rates between boys and girls during the first year of life [citation:txt10]. However, as public health interventions have improved and infant and child mortality rates have declined, the main sources of the gap have shifted to mortality differences in older age groups [citation:txt6]. Today, the sex gap is largely driven by higher male mortality in middle and older adulthood, particularly due to chronic diseases such as heart disease, cancer, and lifestyle-related conditions like smoking and alcohol abuse [citation:txt7].

The size and sources of the sex gap in life expectancy vary significantly between countries. In some nations, such as Japan and Sweden, the gap is relatively small and stable, while in others, like Russia and China, it has been marked by dramatic fluctuations and larger disparities [citation:img2]. These differences are influenced by a range of factors, including national health policies, cultural norms, economic development, and gender-specific health behaviors [citation:txt17]. For example, in countries where smoking rates among men have historically been high, the impact on male mortality has played a central role in shaping the life expectancy gap [citation:txt18].

Over time, the sex gap has also shown a tendency to narrow, particularly in high-income countries. This narrowing is largely attributed to changing health behaviors, especially in relation to smoking and alcohol consumption. As more women have adopted behaviors that were previously more common among men, such as smoking, the delayed health consequences have started to close the gap [citation:txt2]. Additionally, improvements in healthcare access and treatment for chronic diseases have contributed to a reduction in the male mortality advantage at older ages [citation:txt17].

In conclusion, the sex gap in life expectancy is a dynamic and evolving phenomenon. While biological factors play a foundational role, the majority of the gap can be attributed to non-biological influences such as lifestyle choices, social roles, and environmental conditions. Understanding the historical shifts and current variations in the gap is essential for developing targeted public health policies that address the specific needs of men and women across different stages of life [citation:txt1]. As the global landscape of health continues to change, ongoing research and policy innovation will be critical in further reducing disparities and improving life expectancy for all.
